10065-the-constitution-of-the-united-sta:
James M. Beck, Solicitor-General of the United States and honorary bencher of Gray's Inn, wrote this brief study of the Constitution's genesis, formulation, and political philosophy. A preface by the Earl of Balfour introduces the work, which takes Proverbs as its motto: where there is no vision, the people perish.

Beck traces how the Constitution was made and what ideas shaped it, for readers who want the document's story rather than a lawyer's commentary. His tone is reverent and clear. Students of American government get a compact, early twentieth-century account of the founding charter.
10131-required-poems-for-reading-and-mem:
This school book gathers required poems for reading and memorizing in the third and fourth grades, as prescribed by state courses of study. Its poems are chosen to be learned by heart as well as read aloud, building memory and taste together.

Among them are Robert Louis Stevenson's Autumn Fires, with autumn bonfires in other gardens and all up the vale. Short, musical, and clear, the selections suit young voices. Teachers and parents get a period anthology of what American schoolchildren were expected to know by heart. The poems reward voices that learn them well.
10618-jesus-says-so-or-a-memorial-of-lit:
Published in Boston in 1851 by the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, this short religious memorial tells the life of a poor London girl called Sarah G. Her father was hurt in an accident early in 1847 and spent weeks in hospital, leaving the family short of food and help. Sarah, quiet and obedient at home, bore the hardship without complaint.

The account follows her faith as she grows, her kindness to her family, and her early death, which revealed a depth of belief others had not seen. Written for Sunday school readers, it holds Sarah up as a model of patience and trust. It also gives a plain window onto poverty, illness, and church life in London in the 1840s.
11760-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-1:
Compiled by Grenville Kleiser with help from leading preachers, the tenth volume of a 1908 sermon anthology gathers eleven addresses, from Henry Drummond to John Henry Jowett. Each sermon opens with a short biographical note on its preacher, followed by the full text and a general index to preachers and scripture passages.

Drummond's address on love as the greatest thing in the world leads the set. Later sermons take up assurance in God, the Bible against unbelief, and the reconciliation of humanity with God. Read together, they show late Victorian and Edwardian preaching at its most earnest, aimed at ordinary readers rather than scholars alone.
17170-a-study-of-pueblo-pottery-as-illus:
Frank Hamilton Cushing's Bureau of Ethnology study traces Zuni culture growth through pueblo pottery. Chapters show homes shaped by land: round houses to rectangles, flat and terraced roofs from mesa sites, added stories from cliff limits, and communal pueblos from gathered tribes. Pottery follows the same path, from basketry and clay-lined baskets to forms, firing, and decoration.

Figures show hogans, round houses, cliff dwellings, terraced pueblos, and gourd vessels in wicker. Cushing links pots to houses, land, and ritual in a bold, early theory of growth. Students of Southwest peoples will find a classic, richly pictured study of how craft and culture grew together.
17956-recreation-by-viscount-grey-of-fal:
Viscount Grey of Fallodon gave Recreation as an address at the Harvard Union on December 8, 1919, printed in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in 1920. Grey, a British statesman, asks why an age of plenty seems so full of discontent.

He doubts that ours is a pleasure-finding age, despite films, motor cars, and wealth. He names four things that make for happiness: a moral standard, a good home life, work that justifies life, and true recreation. The address is calm, wise, and short, a classic plea for leisure well used, and still apt for readers who chase fun and miss joy.
17970-the-olden-time-series-vol-1-curios:
Henry M. Brooks made this first volume of the Olden-Time Series from old Boston and Salem newspapers, sources few readers could reach. The series aimed to feed a growing taste for quaint notes of ye olden time, in small, cheap handbooks that were both fun and instructive.

This volume gathers curiosities of the old lottery, when towns and colleges raised funds by chance draws. Later volumes would cover spinning-wheels, strange punishments, quaint ads, and literary oddities. Brooks writes with a light, antiquarian charm. It is a pleasant dip into early New England print, best read in short bites.
18534-the-hurricane-guide-being-an-attem:
William Radcliff Birt wrote this hurricane guide, published by John Murray in London in 1850, publisher to the Admiralty. Birt attempts to connect the rotatory gale with atmospheric waves. He gives instructions for observing waves and storms, with practical directions for avoiding storm centers. A pocket in the book holds two rings of stiff cardboard, to be laid on a chart without breaking the continuity of its lines.

Chapters treat phenomena of revolving storms, phenomena of atmospheric waves, and observations, with instruments, times, localities, seasons, and storms, hurricanes, and typhoons. Practical directions for avoiding storm centers close the guide. Birt writes for seamen of Her Majesty's navy and merchant service, who must watch sky and sea to live. Readers get Victorian storm science in usable form: theory, instruments, and rules for keeping a ship out of a hurricane's heart.
24665-a-soldier-s-life-being-the-persona:
Edwin G. Rundle, late sergeant-major in Her Majesty's Leicestershire Regiment of Foot, wrote these personal reminiscences, published at Toronto in 1909 in an author's edition. Rundle had served as instructor and lecturer to the Military School at Toronto from 1866 to 1868, and he was a member of the Red River Expedition.

Major Henry J. Woodside introduces the book, noting the many recent histories of Britain's imperial wars. Rundle's own story gives the soldier's view from the ranks, with drill, service, and campaign life. Readers of military history will find it a plain, lively memoir of a Victorian non-commissioned officer.
28758-philosophical-transactions-of-the-:
This volume collects the first year of the Royal Society's journal, covering 1665 and 1666, printed in London for the Society's printers. The Philosophical Transactions was the world's first journal devoted to new science, and its early numbers report what learned men were doing across Europe: experiments, instruments, observations, and letters between natural philosophers.

Readers meet science in its first draft form, with short reports rather than finished theories, and a dedication to the Society that frames the whole effort. The old spelling and plain reports give a direct sense of how the scientific community first learned to share results in print. For historians of science, it is a ground-floor record of the Royal Society's founding years.
28823-the-works-of-george-meredith-a-lin:
Edited by David Widger, this linked index covers the Project Gutenberg editions of George Meredith's works. The index gathers Meredith's novels, including The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, Sandra Belloni, and Rhoda Fleming. Evan Harrington, Vittoria, Harry Richmond, Beauchamp's Career, and Diana of the Crossways follow, with full chapter lists for each. His short works and The Shaving of Shagpat appear as well.

The volume is a map rather than a novel: it lets readers find their way through Meredith's long and difficult books, chapter by chapter. Meredith, a leading Victorian novelist, wrote complex prose about love, class, and English society, and this index helps a modern reader plan a path through it. It pairs with the Gutenberg texts to make his whole shelf navigable from one file.
29483-the-little-brown-hen-hears-the-son:
Jasmine Stone Van Dresser wrote this 1908 children's book, printed by Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco and New York, with pictures by William T. Van Dresser. Its heroine, a little brown hen, hears the song of the nightingale and finds a golden harvest. An introduction by Margaret Beecher White frames the tales, and a motto warns that the loudest talkers are not always wisest.

The gander in one tale insists the hen must learn his language, calling her chatter silly and drilling all to say honk. Van Dresser's fables teach listening, humility, and kindness through barnyard talk. Young readers and lovers of old picture books will find a gentle, beautifully made volume of animal tales.
31415-stained-glass-work-a-text-book-for:
C. W. Whall's Stained Glass Work, a text-book for students and workers in glass, belongs to the Artistic Crafts Series of technical handbooks edited by W. R. Lethaby and published by D. Appleton and Company of New York. Whall, with diagrams by two of his apprentices and other illustrations, covers the craft in two parts, from design and glass cutting to glazing, as the frontispiece on cutting and glazing shows. The book is a working manual, not a history.

Whall writes for makers: students learning the trade and workers already at the bench. His instructions are practical, covering materials, tools, leading, and painting on glass. For readers interested in the Arts and Crafts movement, the book shows a master craftsman passing on a medieval art in modern workshop terms, with clarity and pride in good work.
31843-of-six-medi-val-women-to-which-is-:
Alice Kemp-Welch's 1913 book Of Six Mediaeval Women, with a note on mediaeval gardens, published by Macmillan, studies six women across six centuries. They are Roswitha the nun, tenth-century dramatist; Marie de France, twelfth-century romance writer; and Mechthild of Magdeburg, thirteenth-century mystic and Beguine. The others are Mahaut, Countess of Artois, fourteenth-century art patron; Christine de Pisan, fifteenth-century feminist; and Agnes Sorel.

Illustrations include Roswitha presenting her poem to Emperor Otho the First, a lady playing the harp, and a banquet with minstrels. Readers get a pioneering work of women's history, recovering writers, patrons, and mystics whom older histories had passed over.
32595-a-woman-s-wartime-journal-an-accou:
Dolly Sumner Lunt, writing as Mrs. Thomas Burge, kept this diary on her Georgia plantation through the Civil War, here with an introduction and notes by Julian Street. Entries run from January 1864, when prices soar and war still rages, into late 1865.

Lunt records cannon fire near Atlanta, flight on the roads, and frantic efforts to hide mules, meat, and clothes from troops. When Sherman's army passes her house, it tears down fences and cuts a road through her yard, and her plain daily notes show war as a household ordeal.
a-study-of-pueblo-pottery-as-illustrativ: Frank Hamilton Cushing studies Pueblo pottery as a guide to Zuni ways of life, in this paper from the Bureau of Ethnology's fourth annual report. The contents trace homes shaped by their surrounds, square forms from round ones, stepped roofs from sloping mesa sites, and shared pueblos from cliff-house tribes. Pottery follows the same logic. Seen first in basketry and hinted at by clay-lined basketry, it is shaped by its earth, its firing, its form, its paint, and its signs.
doe-osti-2573966-high-performance-solven: A hot solvent for gas-plant CO2 capture got its DOE final, and this report covers NGCC flue gas capture. The pages detail the solvent performance. The carbon capturers get their recipe. The report was final technical. The gas was flue.
doe-osti-3000013-lower-snake-river-dams-: Lower Snake River dams got their grid study, and this DOE report covers their grid services. The pages detail the contributions. The grid planners get their numbers. The dams were Lower Snake River. The numbers were planner. The study was grid.
doe-osti-3000792-second-generation-non-a: Gen2NAS solvents got their second generation, and this DOE report captures CO2 from gas plants. The pages detail the non-aqueous findings. The carbon folks get their option. The solvents were second generation. The capture was natural gas. The plants were gas.
doe-osti-3018250-communications-reliabil: Vehicle-grid comms got reliability-tested, and this DOE text covers integration. The pages detail the findings. The grid folks get their data. The integration was vehicle grid. The data were grid. The grid was vehicle. The reliability was communications.
doe-osti-3020301-em-porin-inspired-ionom: Porin ionomers got sub-nm-gated, and this DOE final builds ion channels. The pages detail the findings. The materials folks get their closeout. The conductivity was high ion. The closeout was material. The channels were ion. The nm was sub.
doe-osti-3362555-key-performance-indicat: Vehicle grid got KPI'd, and this DOE text covers integration indicators. The pages detail the performance findings. The transport folks get their data. The integration was vehicle grid. The data were transport. The indicators were key. The grid were vehicle.
doe-osti-3363716-resstock-measure-docume: ResStock got gas-furnace-documented, and this DOE measure covers 95% AFUE. The pages detail the natural findings. The building folks get their data. The furnace was gas. The data were building. The AFUE were 95%. The gas were furnace. The building were folks.
doe-osti-3364915-resstock-measure-docume: ResStock got gas-heater-documented, and this DOE measure covers natural gas water. The pages detail the findings. The building folks get their data. The heater was water. The data were building. The gas were natural. The heater were water.
doe-osti-3375449-multi-material-hydrodyn: Ghost Fluid got hydrodynamics-slid, and this DOE text covers multi-material slides. The pages detail the method findings. The physicists get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was physicist. The fluid were ghost. The slides were format.
doe-osti-3380282-recycle-ga-from-e-waste: Ga got e-waste-recycled, and this DOE final CRADA covers GaN chips. The pages detail the recycle findings. The materials folks get their closeout. The prize was American-made. The closeout was material. The GaAs were chips. The voucher were prize.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAFassnachtGeo:
George E. Fassnacht had worked for the CIA, and by January 1975 he was in court trying to get his arsenal back. Dave Racher reported for the Philadelphia Daily News on January 20 that Fassnacht had lost his bid to recover what the government had seized.

The seized stock was not a hunter's cabinet: machine guns, explosives, and 363,000 rounds of ammunition. Cases like his fed the era's fascination with former intelligence men and their private arsenals after Watergate. The single article is preserved as a newspaper record of the judgment and the strange inventory behind it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimDoJG: Floyd D. Moore of the Internal Revenue Service swore an affidavit in June 1971 in support of a complaint and search warrants. The filing belongs to the federal government's case touching New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison, whose name heads the archive file. The surviving record gives the agent, his agency, and the month, but not the affidavit's charges in detail.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LatinAmericaGen: Charles Keeley of United Press International wrote 'South America: Armies in Command,' a wire-service survey of the continent's military governments. The piece belongs to the era when generals ruled much of South America and wire reporters summed up the pattern for American readers. The file gives the title, the author, and the subject, but no date and no further detail about which countries the survey covered or what it concluded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LawsonWinstonG_:
A researcher compiled these notes on the official statement of Winston Lawson, a Secret Service agent who worked on the Dallas motorcade. The notes run to five pages on Lawson's account. They take up the Air Force One passenger manifest, the first shot as the motorcade passed under the overpass, and the emergency-room response at the hospital.

Lawson's statement formed part of the record the Warren Commission relied on. A private researcher's notes show the other side of that record: readers outside government checking each claim against the rest of the file. The notes record what one close reader found important in Lawson's words, and what he found doubtful.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NorthrupWilliam:
On January 25, 1968, the office of Senator Robert F. Kennedy answered a mailing from William G. Northrup. Northrup had sent his booklet, 'The Overlooked Factor, Or — A Rendezvous With Death!' The senator's office acknowledged receiving it, in the form letter such mailings drew.

Citizens mailed theories to senators by the sackful in those years, and Kennedy's office received more than most. Four months later, Kennedy himself was assassinated. A polite acknowledgment is thin evidence of anything but receipt. Still, the letter preserves the traffic: a self-published booklet with a dramatic title, sent to a senator, logged and answered by staff while the events it worried about were still unfolding.
nasa-tm-19660026439-solar-evolution-with:
D. Ezer and A. G. W. Cameron, at the Institute for Space Studies in New York, ask a bold question in this paper. What if gravity itself has slowly changed over time? They test that idea, called varying-G cosmology, by recalculating how the Sun evolved under it.

Their model sequence extends their earlier work on early solar evolution. In the varying-G Sun, they find, lithium is used up less than in a constant-G Sun. The time to burn out the central hydrogen also shrinks, helped by much greater helium production. Their present-day model predicts a far higher neutrino output, a claim they note can be checked by experiment.
nasa-tm-19670009029-calculation-of-densi:
V. A. J. van Lint, Felix E. Geiger Jr., and D. K. Nichols describe a calculation method in this paper. Gamma rays passing through a material knock electrons loose, and those electrons damage the material's crystal structure. The authors show how to calculate the density of such defects to be expected.

Their method uses measured rates at which defects appear. It also uses the range-energy curve for electrons and the theoretical spectrum of Compton electrons. They work a specific case: silicon exposed to cobalt-60 gamma rays. Their result agrees reasonably with experimental data, and it corrects an earlier theoretical calculation.
nasa-tm-19680001779-compression-of-the-p:
H. A. Taylor Jr., H. C. Brinton, and M. W. Pharo III, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It studies the compression of the plasmasphere during geomagnetically disturbed periods. The plasmasphere is the fat torus of cold plasma co-rotating around Earth, and magnetic storms squeeze it inward.

Positive ion mass spectrometers aboard the OGO I and OGO III satellites measured hydrogen and helium ions directly during 1965 and 1966. Inside the plasmasphere, ion concentration fell gradually with height, but at the outer boundary, the plasmapause, it dropped abruptly. Sometimes it fell tenfold within a few hundred kilometers. That boundary moved inward and outward in step with planetary magnetic activity, showing large-scale expansion and contraction. During one stormy stretch in July 1966, the boundary was caught unusually low over the nightside Earth.
nasa-tm-19710015486-cosmic-antimatter-an:
F. W. Stecker, D. L. Morgan, and J. Bredekamp of the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in April 1971, numbered X-641-71-150. It asks whether antimatter exists on a large scale in the universe. When matter meets antimatter, both are destroyed and gamma rays result, so a cosmic gamma-ray glow could betray hidden antimatter.

The authors present early results from a detailed calculation of the gamma-ray spectrum that such annihilation would produce across the cosmos. Their calculated spectrum closely resembles the observed background above one million electron volts. They read that match as possible evidence for large-scale antimatter. The calculation folds in annihilation cross sections, absorption by the intergalactic medium, and photon scattering at high redshifts.
nasa-tm-19710025480-note-on-the-characte:
Kunitomo Sakurai wrote this note in July 1971, numbered X-693-71-267, on the sunspot groups that produce solar proton flares. Sakurai was a NASA associate with the University of Maryland. Most sunspot groups stay quiet, but a few erupt and spray high-energy protons into space, endangering astronauts and spacecraft.

The note argues that the production of solar cosmic rays grows as the gradient, the steepness, of a group's magnetic field increases. Such steep gradients form along with the rotating motion of sunspot groups. Groups whose polarity pattern is reversed prove especially effective at producing proton flares. Sakurai builds on Severny's work, which sorted proton flares into four classes tied to the magnetic field gradient.
podcast-dannyjones-uPTYwIEWH-g:
Shane Lee of the Deck Hands crew sits with Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 8. The session starts in chaos over headphones and gear. Lee would rather skip the fancy setup entirely.

Once settled, the talk turns to boats, work, and the crew's rough humor. Lee tells tales from life on the water near Florida. The tape keeps false starts and swearing in place. That rawness is the point of the early KONCRETE shows. The episode preserves a deckhand's voice before polish, fame, or sponsors smoothed anything out. Lee never tries to sound polished or grand.
podcast-joerogan-2k8xnF1tg-g:
Comedian Dave Landau joins Joe Rogan for episode 2373. Landau is known for dark jokes and a dry delivery. He has drawn praise as a sharp stand-up in the style of past greats.

Early talk turns to Detroit and how the city fell and rose. Landau notes it was once among the richest cities on earth. The pair trade stories about clubs, crowds, and hard years on the road. The episode mixes city history with shop talk from two men who have spent their lives on stage and behind microphones.
podcast-joerogan-6DQSIzJ9J-g:
Do the beings people meet on DMT count as real? Rogan takes up the famous question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Users of the drug often report meeting playful entities, sometimes called elves, and many insist the beings felt more real than waking life.

Rogan turns the reports over from every side: brain chemistry, shared hallucination, or a door to somewhere else. He draws on his own long interest in the drug and the stories guests have told him. The segment cannot settle the matter, but it states the puzzle well, in the words of a host who has chased it for years.
podcast-joerogan-Lb_1d68vx-g:
Bob Lazar returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2479, this time with Luigi Vendittelli beside him. Lazar's 1989 claims about working on alien craft near Area 51 made him the most famous whistleblower in UFO culture. His first Rogan visit was a landmark for the show.

The talk revisits his story with years of new attention layered on top, including fresh claims and fresh scrutiny. Rogan asks what has changed and what Lazar still cannot prove. For followers of the case, the episode is the latest full statement from a man whose account has been argued over for decades.
podcast-joerogan-m7Hrq8WL1-g:
Warren Smith talks with Rogan for episode 2261 of the Joe Rogan Experience, in a long and open conversation. The entry keeps the full talk as aired, with the guest across hours in the show's standard unscripted form.

The transcript holds the whole back-and-forth, so readers meet the guest's stories and views whole rather than trimmed. Full sittings like this one are the show's basic record, and the library keeps them complete. The episode is filed for listeners and fans who want the entire appearance on file, from the first exchange to the last.
podcast-joerogan-pVbygFFBJ_g:
Joe Rogan roams through brain implants, Iron Man suits, and robot children in a segment from his show. The three topics share one theme: the merge of man and machine. Rogan hosts the tour of what labs now build.

Rogan works through chips that let minds move cursors, suits that grant huge strength, and bots raised to seem like kids. He asks where the line of the human sits as the merge grows. The segment is short and full of awe and doubt. Listeners get a brisk tour of the cyborg age. The library holds the file as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rsSmQEJyO-g:
Tucker Carlson reports that the global war on Christians has grown worse and names Senator Ted Cruz as a man who does not care. The episode title makes both the charge and the call-out. Carlson speaks in his own voice.

Carlson lays out fresh cases of Christians jailed, killed, or driven from their homes across the world. He argues US leaders shrug while faith dies abroad. He singles out Cruz for praise of Israel while Christians there suffer, as Carlson sees it. Listeners get the full charge in one place. The library keeps it as a record of his stated view.
recreation-by-viscount-grey-of-fallodon-:
Viscount Grey of Fallodon, K.G., spoke on recreation at the Harvard Union on December 8, 1919, and Houghton Mifflin printed the address in 1920. He doubts at the start that his is a pleasure-finding age, for all its wealth and new amusements. Moving pictures and motor-cars abound, yet content seems scarce and discontent grows.

Grey asks what makes people happy and what they can do to make themselves so. Recreation is one part of happiness, not the chief part, he grants. He names a moral standard to guide one's acts as the first of four other things in our own control, with good home life next.
required-poems-for-reading-and-memorizin:
State courses of study prescribed these poems for reading and memorizing in the third and fourth grades. The set opens with poems by Robert Louis Stevenson. Autumn Fires comes first, picturing bonfires in the gardens and up the vale, their grey smoke towering as summer ends.

Its refrain bids children sing a song of seasons, finding something bright in all. The Unseen Playmate follows, about the Friend of the Children who comes out of the wood when children play alone. No one hears or sees him, the poem says, yet he sings when a child tinkles a musical glass. Later poets in the set fall beyond the pages shown.
the-constitution-of-the-united-states-a-: James M. Beck was solicitor-general of the United States and an honorary bencher of Gray's Inn. He wrote this brief study of the birth, framing, and guiding ideas of the United States Constitution. The Earl of Balfour supplies a preface. Beck dedicates the book to Attorney-General Harry M. Daugherty, dated from Chamonix on July 14, 1922. Balfour's preface recalls Beck's wartime writing for the Allied cause. Only the front matter and the start of that preface are present here.
the-hurricane-guide-being-an-attempt-to-:
William Radcliff Birt published this guide with John Murray of London in 1850. Murray was publisher to the Admiralty. The full title states the project plainly. It connects the rotatory gale with atmospheric waves. It gives instructions for observing both. Practical directions help sailors avoid storm centers. The preface states his aim clearly. He wants to show a link between two phenomena. One is among the most terrific on the globe. The other is little known but closely bound to storms.

Birt leaves the argument's success to the public. His second aim is plain enough. Seamen should learn the essential facts of storms. A mid-century sailor had no forecasts. Reading wave and weather signs could save his ship. It could decide whether he skirted a hurricane or sailed into its center. The book turns storm science into working rules.
the-olden-time-series-vol-1-curiosities-: Curiosities of the Old Lottery is volume 1 of the Olden Time Series, small handbooks prepared by Henry M. Brooks and sold by Ticknor and Company of Boston at 50 cents. Only the publisher's series pages and the title page are present here, so the lottery pieces themselves do not appear. The same series pages open the other Olden Time volumes in this group. Brooks gathered his material chiefly from old Boston and Salem newspapers, and a Salem Gazette notice praises his collecting.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-10-drum: The final volume of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser in 1908, is represented by its contents list. Henry Drummond leads with The Greatest Thing in the World. A general index to the ten volumes is included. Other preachers named include Gordon, Dawson, and Gunsaulus. Hillis contributes God the Unwearied Guide. The sermons themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
